# Canon: parse-alloy

How parse-alloy reads Alloy, and why. It is the canon of the package `@bigmistqke/parse-alloy`. The syntax it follows is that of the Alloy analyzer 6.2.0 (`794226d`): `Alloy.cup`, `Alloy.lex` and `CompFilter.java`.

## Terms

### @term parsed-formula

> A parsed formula is a formula as the parser reads it: its operators, their operands and their grouping.

## @axiom alloy-is-read-as-the-analyzer-reads-it

> parse-alloy reads Alloy exactly as the Alloy analyzer reads it: every formula grouped as the analyzer groups it. It refuses, with the place and the reason, anything it cannot read that way.

This follows because a tool that builds on the tree, such as naturalloy saying a formula in words, inherits every mistake in it. A formula grouped otherwise than the analyzer groups it means something else, and nothing downstream can notice. A refusal is better than a wrong tree.

#### @spec a-formula-the-parser-cannot-read-is-refused-and-the-refusal-names-what-it-cannot-read

> The parser refuses a [formula](#term-parsed-formula) with a construct, a stray character or an unclosed bracket that it cannot read, and names it.

This follows because a tree of part of a formula means less than the formula. The author must know which part failed.

#### @spec a-quantifier-takes-everything-after-its-bar

> The parser reads everything after the bar of a quantifier as its body, up to a `;`.

This follows because the bar ends the declaration, and what follows is the claim about the variables. The analyzer ends the body at a `;`.

#### @spec a-temporal-operator-takes-the-formula-next-to-it

> The parser reads the formula next to a temporal operator as its operand.

This follows because the analyzer binds `always`, `eventually`, `after` and the other unary temporal operators as tightly as `not`.

#### @spec a-semicolon-takes-everything-after-it

> The parser reads the formula after a `;` as everything that follows it, and the formula before it as everything back to the start, `implies` and `or` included. After the bar of a quantifier, the formula before it is the quantifier.

This follows because the Alloy analyzer binds the semicolon looser than every connective and groups it to the right.

#### @spec disj-before-the-variables-of-a-quantifier-is-read

> The parser reads `disj` before the variables of a declaration as a mark on that declaration.

This follows because `disj` belongs to the declaration it stands before.

#### @spec and-binds-tighter-than-implies

> The parser reads an `and` beside an `implies` before the `implies`.

This follows because the analyzer binds `and` tighter than `implies`.

#### @spec a-chain-of-and-is-one-list

> The parser reads a chain of `and` as one list.

This follows because three conditions joined by and are one list of three, and not an and of an and.

#### @spec not-in-a-join-a-prime-and-a-call-are-read

> The parser reads `not in`, a join, a prime and a call.

This follows because each is part of the syntax the analyzer reads.

#### @spec some-of-a-set-is-a-multiplicity

> The parser reads `some` before a set as a statement about the set, and not as a quantifier.

This follows because some followed by a set says the set is not empty, and it declares no variable.

#### @spec some-with-a-declaration-is-a-quantifier

> The parser reads `some` before variables and a bar as a quantifier over those variables.

This follows because some followed by variables and a bar declares those variables.
